Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection on EO Imagery¶

MLP Autoencoder vs 1D CNN Autoencoder (Pavia University HSI Dataset)

Objective¶

This notebook presents anomaly detection in hyperspectral Earth Observation imagery using reconstruction-based models.

We evaluate:

  • MLP autoencoder (global spectral modeling)
  • 1D CNN autoencoder (local spectral modeling)

Goal: understand how model design affects anomaly detection performance under a controlled setup.

Workflow¶

  1. Data loading and inspection
  2. Image preprocessing
  3. Model training (2 architectures)
  4. Evaluation and comparison (OA, F1, IoU, and ROC AUC)
  5. Prediction visualization

Dataset¶

We use a subset of the Pavia University hyperspectral image dataset.

  • hyperspectral urban scene
  • 610 × 340 pixels, 103 spectral bands
  • ground truth with multiple land-cover classes

The dataset is not originally designed for anomaly detection; anomalies are defined from selected ground-truth classes.

Training and testing regions are spatially separated.

Data Inspection¶

Visual inspection to verify class distribution, spatial structure, and ground truth coverage.

Image Preprocessing¶

  • Spectral bands are normalized independently to reduce scale differences across channels.
  • The anomaly target is defined from the ground-truth label map: Class 5 = Painted metal sheets.
  • A normal-only training region and an anomaly-containing test region are selected manually to simulate unsupervised anomaly detection.
In [6]:
# Normalize data per band 
h, w, c = data.shape
X = data.reshape(-1, c).astype(np.float32)
band_min = X.min(axis=0)
band_max = X.max(axis=0)
X = (X - band_min) / (band_max - band_min + 1e-6)
data_norm = X.reshape(h, w, c)

# Define anomaly mask 
# Class 5 = painted metal sheets

mask = (gt == anomaly_class).astype(np.uint8)

In [8]:
# Dataset wrapper for hyperspectral anomaly detection
# - Training: uses only normal-region pixels (no anomaly mask)
# - Testing: uses all pixels with corresponding anomaly labels
class HSIAnomalyDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, mask=None, train=True):
        """
        X: (h, w, c) hyperspectral cube (already normalized)
        mask: (h, w) anomaly mask (for test set only)
        train: True for training (only normal pixels), False for testing (all pixels)
        """
        h, w, c = X.shape
        self.X = X.reshape(-1, c)
        self.mask = mask.reshape(-1) if mask is not None else None
        self.train = train

        self.indices = np.arange(len(self.X))

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.indices)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        i = self.indices[idx]
        x = torch.tensor(self.X[i], dtype=torch.float32)
        if self.train:
            return x
        else:
            y = torch.tensor(self.mask[i], dtype=torch.long)
            return x, y

# Construct datasets from spatially cropped train/test regions
train_ds = HSIAnomalyDataset(train_data, train=True)
test_ds  = HSIAnomalyDataset(test_data, mask=test_mask, train=False)

train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=512, shuffle=True)
test_loader  = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=2048, shuffle=False)

print(f"Train pixels: {len(train_ds)} | Test pixels: {len(test_ds)} | Anomalies (test): {test_mask.sum()}")

Train pixels: 4800 | Test pixels: 11700 | Anomalies (test): 1345

Model Training (2 Architectures)¶

We compare two reconstruction-based autoencoders under the same training and evaluation pipeline:

  • MLP Autoencoder: learns global relationships across the full spectral vector.
  • 1D CNN Autoencoder: learns local neighboring patterns along the spectral dimension using convolutional filters.
In [9]:
# Autoencoder - MLP 
class MLPAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(in_dim, 128), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, 32), nn.ReLU()
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(32, 128), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, in_dim), nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.decoder(self.encoder(x))

# Autoencoder - 1D CNN 
# kernel_size=3 → each filter sees 3 adjacent spectral bands (local context)
class CNNAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(1, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv1d(16, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(8, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv1d(16, 1, kernel_size=3, padding=1), nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.unsqueeze(1)
        z = self.encoder(x)
        out = self.decoder(z)
        return out.squeeze(1)


def build_model(model_name, in_dim):
    if model_name == "mlp":
        return MLPAE(in_dim)
    elif model_name == "cnn1d":
        return CNNAE(in_dim)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown model_name: {model_name}")
In [10]:
# Unified training setup
model_name = "mlp"   # "mlp" | "cnn1d"

in_dim = train_data.shape[-1] # number of input features (spectral bands)
model = build_model(model_name, in_dim).to(device)

criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)

EPOCHS = 50

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    model.train()
    epoch_loss = 0.0

    for batch in train_loader:
        batch = batch.to(device)

        out = model(batch)
        loss = criterion(out, batch)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        epoch_loss += loss.item()

    epoch_loss /= len(train_loader)

    if (epoch + 1) % 10 == 0 or epoch == 0 or epoch == EPOCHS - 1:
        print(f"[{model_name.upper()} | Epoch {epoch+1:02d}/{EPOCHS}] Loss: {epoch_loss:.6f}")

Evaluation¶

  • ROC-AUC / PR-AUC — threshold-independent separability of reconstruction scores (normal vs anomaly)
  • F1 (anomaly) — primary metric; reflects detection quality under strong class imbalance
  • IoU (normal / anomaly) — spatial overlap; highlights boundary errors and fragmented predictions
  • mIoU — overall segmentation consistency across classes
  • OA — reported for reference, but not reliable under imbalance
In [11]:
# Final evaluation
model.eval()
scores, labels = [], []

with torch.no_grad():
    for x, y in test_loader:  
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        out = model(x)
        # reconstruction error per pixel: MSE over spectral bands (C-dimension)
        loss = ((out - x) ** 2).mean(dim=1) 
        scores.extend(loss.cpu().numpy())
        labels.extend(y.cpu().numpy())

scores = np.array(scores)
labels = np.array(labels, dtype=np.int64)

# ROC-AUC & PR-AUC
roc_auc = roc_auc_score(labels, scores)
pr_auc  = average_precision_score(labels, scores)

# Select decision threshold that maximizes F1 score
best_f1, best_th = 0, 0.0
for th in np.linspace(scores.min(), scores.max(), 100):
    pred = (scores > th).astype(int)
    f1 = f1_score(labels, pred)
    if f1 > best_f1:
        best_f1, best_th = f1, th

pred = (scores > best_th).astype(int)
cm = confusion_matrix(labels, pred, labels=[0,1])
oa = np.diag(cm).sum()/cm.sum()
iou = np.diag(cm)/(cm.sum(1)+cm.sum(0)-np.diag(cm)+1e-6)

print("======== Evaluation ========")
print(f"ROC-AUC    : {roc_auc:.3f} | PR-AUC : {pr_auc:.3f}")
print()

print(f"OA         : {oa:.3f} | F1     : {best_f1:.3f}")
print(f"IoU        : normal {iou[0]:.3f}, anomaly {iou[1]:.3f}")
print(f"mIoU       : {iou.mean():.3f}")
print()

print(f"Score range: {scores.min():.2e} → {scores.max():.3f}")
print(f"Threshold  : {best_th:.5f}")
print(f"Anomaly px : pred {pred.sum()}, gt {labels.sum()}")

Experimental Notes¶

  • The MLP autoencoder converged quickly; increasing epochs beyond 50 provided negligible gains for both models.
  • Adam with a learning rate of 1e-2 performed best; smaller or larger values degraded performance.
  • AdamW, SGD, StepLR, and cosine decay did not yield improvements.
  • The 1D CNN autoencoder underperformed the MLP, suggesting that global spectral structure is more informative than local spectral patterns in this setup.
  • Detection performance is governed by spectral separability from the training distribution; classes with distinct spectral signatures are easier to detect.

Sensitivity Analysis — Different Ground Truth Classes as Anomalies¶

We fix the trained model (vegetation-dominated training region) and evaluate sensitivity by redefining the anomaly label: each ground-truth class is treated as the anomaly in turn.

Class Name Pixels (test) F1 Interpretation
0 Background 8996 0.87 heterogeneous composition; strongly deviates from vegetation baseline
5 Painted metal sheets 1345 0.78 strong spectral contrast relative to vegetation
2 Meadows 768 0.12 spectrally aligned with training distribution
1 Asphalt 300 0.09 partial spectral overlap with learned normal features
8 Self-blocking bricks 21 0.01 low contrast; high similarity to surrounding materials

Note — pixel counts refer to the test region; classes with low support yield less reliable F1 estimates.

Performance degrades as class spectra become more aligned with the training distribution.

Model localizes the main anomalous structures reliably; errors concentrate at object boundaries and in small isolated false positives. The anomaly score map clearly highlights the metal-sheet structures, with residual errors arising from boundary ambiguity due to annotation tightness, spectral similarity in surrounding materials, and illumination variation.

Model Comparison¶

Model Input Modeling OA F1 (anom) IoU (anom) PR AUC ROC AUC Strength Limitation
MLP AE Global (full vector) 0.94 0.78 0.64 0.80 0.98 Captures full spectral signature Ignores local continuity
1D CNN AE Local (kernel=3) 0.91 0.49 0.32 0.47 0.78 Learns local spectral patterns Misses long-range spectral dependencies

Key Observation

  • The MLP autoencoder consistently outperforms the 1D CNN autoencoder across F1, IoU (anomaly), and PR AUC. This indicates that anomaly separability is primarily driven by global spectral signature, rather than short-range local correlations.

  • The 1D CNN, constrained to local neighborhoods (kernel size = 3, i.e., three adjacent spectral bands), captures smooth spectral variations but fails to model long-range dependencies across the full spectrum, which are critical for distinguishing anomalous materials.

Conclusion¶

In this controlled setting, global spectral reconstruction is more effective than local convolutional filtering for anomaly detection. This suggests that anomalies are characterized by holistic spectral deviations rather than localized band-to-band variations.

A simple reconstruction-based autoencoder provides a strong baseline for hyperspectral anomaly detection. In this experiment, tuning the learning rate improved performance more than increasing model complexity. The best result came from the MLP autoencoder, while the 1D CNN did not improve detection.

This suggests that, in this Pavia University anomaly setting, global spectral reconstruction is more effective than local spectral filtering.
